strengths: Clear and well-motivated central insight: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias for AR-based generative classification, illustrated convincingly via Figure 1 and the per-token discriminative likelihood/accuracy analyses in Section 5 (Figs. 3-5).
The proposed order-marginalization scheme (Jensen lower bound over K sampled orders) is simple, well justified empirically, and clearly derived from the any-order RandAR formulation.

Extensive and fair experimental protocol: models are matched in architecture, size, resolution and token count across AR, diffusion, joint-EBM and discriminative baselines; missing checkpoints are reproduced following official implementations, and the authors specifically tune diffusion baselines (loss weighting, noise-sample averaging) to ensure they are not under-optimized (Appendix C, D).

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent gains over diffusion classifiers and other AR classifiers (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC) across ImageNet-Val and multiple OOD/corruption benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), plus real-world distribution-shift evaluation on WILDS (Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW), and efficiency-accuracy curves showing up to 25x speed-up versus DiT.

First comparison of generative classifiers against strong SSL discriminative baselines (DINOv2), showing competitive rather than merely academic performance, which is a meaningful contribution to the ongoing debate on GC viability.
Thorough ablations on tokenizer choice, noise augmentation, likelihood estimation strategy, and per-token contribution analysis (Appendix B), improving reproducibility and interpretability.
Honest error analysis comparing failure modes of RandAR vs. DINOv2, adding useful qualitative insight beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is primarily an application/analysis of an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) rather than a new architecture or training method; the order-marginalization idea, while effective, is a relatively straightforward Monte Carlo/Jensen bound over an already-trained capability.

The justification for why the Jensen lower bound outperforms the direct order-marginal likelihood is largely hypothesized rather than rigorously analyzed ("we hypothesize that the lower bound largely outperforms... because RandAR was trained directly on Equation 5"), leaving the theoretical grounding somewhat underdeveloped.

A key practical limitation acknowledged only in the conclusion (compute scaling with number of classes, since separate forward passes are needed per class and per sampled order) is not empirically analyzed for classification tasks with very large label spaces, limiting insight into practical scalability beyond ImageNet's 1000 classes.

In-domain accuracy still trails DINOv2 (particularly on IN-A), and the paper's framing of "competitive" performance, while defensible, could benefit from more discussion of when generative classifiers would be preferred in practice given their added inference cost even after the reported efficiency gains relative to diffusion.

Evaluation on 2K subsets of some validation/OOD sets (necessitated by compute cost) could raise minor concerns about statistical robustness of fine-grained comparisons, despite the authors' claim that larger subsets yield similar results.

Model scale is limited to L/XL variants; it remains unclear whether the reported trends (order-marginalization benefits, relative gains over diffusion) persist at larger scales or with more modern tokenizers/architectures.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated central insight: fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias for AR-based generative classification, and order marginalization via any-order AR models (RandAR) substantially improves accuracy — this is demonstrated convincingly through Table 1 and the qualitative per-token analyses in Figs 3-5.

Strong and extensive empirical evaluation: comparisons against diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT, SiT+REPA), joint energy models (DAT), other AR baselines (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+), discriminative supervised (ViT) and SOTA SSL (DINOv2) models, across in-domain and multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C), plus WILDS distribution-shift datasets (Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW) and non-image-centric/multi-object datasets (ObjectNet, COCO).

Good efficiency analysis showing up to 25x speedup over diffusion classifiers at comparable or better accuracy, with accuracy-vs-runtime curves across model sizes (Fig 6), which is a practically important contribution given DCs' expensive multi-step likelihood estimation.

Thoughtful ablations: likelihood estimation strategy (lower bound vs direct estimate, Table 5), tokenizer choice and noise augmentation (Tables 3-4), generalization to another any-order architecture (RAR, Table 6 left), and connection to masked diffusion models with theoretical derivation (Appendix D) plus empirical comparison (Table 6 right).

The comparison against SOTA self-supervised discriminative models (DINOv2) is a novel and meaningful benchmark that prior generative-classifier papers have not attempted, adding significance to the contribution.

Extensive appendices addressing many reviewer-anticipated concerns: DM noise averaging (Appendix C), loss weighting ablations for DM baselines (Appendix E), ResNet comparison (Appendix F), REPA variants (Appendix F), few-step diffusion (MeanFlow) comparison (Appendix I), and per-token likelihood importance analysis (Appendix B) — these substantially strengthen the fairness and thoroughness of the empirical claims.
Reasonably good clarity, with a clear framework diagram (Fig 2) and interesting qualitative visualizations of per-token discriminative likelihoods that support the core hypothesis.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the method largely applies an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) with Monte Carlo averaging over the model's own training objective (Eq 5) to classification, without introducing new algorithmic machinery specific to classification (e.g., no learned order selection, no fine-tuning for discrimination). The 'lower bound over direct likelihood' insight is useful but relatively simple in nature.

RandAR-XL still underperforms DINOv2 on in-domain ImageNet accuracy and on IN-A, and the paper's claims of 'competitive' performance rely on cherry-picking specific OOD sets where RandAR wins (3 of 5); a more balanced framing of where generative classifiers still lag is warranted.

The efficiency comparison against diffusion classifiers, while extensive, focuses mainly on standard multi-step DMs; although Appendix I compares to MeanFlow, that comparison shows few-step diffusion classifiers perform much worse, which raises the question whether the diffusion baseline is representative of the strongest possible diffusion-based classifier design (e.g., more efficient ELBO estimators) rather than an artifact of insufficiently optimized few-step likelihood estimation.

K (number of sampled orders) must be fairly large (K=20) to achieve strong performance, which multiplies inference cost roughly 20x relative to a single AR forward pass; although this remains cheaper than DMs, the paper could better contextualize the practical cost/complexity tradeoff for users who might want single-pass efficiency.

The method depends on a specific any-order AR architecture (RandAR) with explicit position-token conditioning; generalization is only lightly validated with one additional architecture (RAR-B) at a single (base) model scale, leaving open questions about whether the approach scales across other any-order or masked generative architectures.

Some of the explanatory hypotheses (e.g., why per-token accuracy peaks at prefix length ~70, why raster order underperforms random K=1) are speculative post-hoc arguments without deeper causal or theoretical validation.

The experiments and analyses are entirely restricted to ImageNet-derived tasks (plus WILDS and COCO/ObjectNet variants at 256x256); scalability to higher-resolution or more complex/multi-domain benchmarks is unexplored, which somewhat limits the demonstrated generality of the classification improvements claimed.
